title: Pressure-cooker split pea soup
subtitle: A thick, satisfying soup from dried peas in 20 minutes
excerpt: Dried split peas cooked under pressure with stock and aromatics into a thick, creamy soup. No soaking needed, no cream required, the peas break down naturally into a velvety result.
sourceNotes: Split pea soup is documented across British, Dutch, and Scandinavian cooking as a winter staple. In Britain, pea and ham soup uses the cooking liquid from a gammon joint as the base. The pressure cooker compresses the usual 1 to 1.5 hour stovetop simmer to about 20 minutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool and freeze in airtight containers for up to 6 months. Reheat with a little stock or water, the soup thickens significantly when cold.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze in individual portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup thickens on standing. Reheat with extra stock to loosen.

content.text: Split pea soup makes the case for dried legumes better than almost any other dish. Green split peas disintegrate completely under pressure into a thick, velvety soup that needs no cream and no blending, the peas do all the work themselves. The pressure cooker compresses a 90-minute stovetop simmer to 20 minutes.

The traditional British version, pea and ham soup, adds the cooking liquid from a gammon joint in place of vegetable stock. If you have cooked gammon recently, the reserved liquid is the best base you can use: salty, porky, and deeply flavoured.
The soup thickens considerably as it stands and cools. Reheat with a splash of stock or water to restore the pourable consistency.

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, and celery; cook for 6 minutes until softened. Add the garlic; stir for 1 minute. Add the rinsed split peas, {{stock-vegetable}} of vegetable stock, bay leaf, and thyme. Season with salt and pepper.

Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 20 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of at least 10 minutes before opening. Open the lid and stir, the peas should have broken down into the broth. Discard the bay and thyme. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

rows.symptom: The soup is very thick and barely pourable
rows.cause: Split peas break down completely and absorb liquid significantly.
rows.fix: Stir in additional hot stock or water to reach the desired consistency.

rows.symptom: Whole peas remain in the soup
rows.cause: The natural pressure release was too short, or the peas were very old.
rows.fix: Return to pressure for a further 10 minutes. Alternatively, blend a portion of the soup to create a smoother result.

rows.symptom: Foam came from the pressure valve
rows.cause: Legume foam is common under pressure.
rows.fix: Split peas tend to foam less than chickpeas or haricot beans, but still add the rinsing step and do not fill the pot more than two-thirds full.

content.text: Split pea soup is deeply satisfying winter food, substantial enough to constitute a meal, cheap to make, and truly warming. The British version with gammon stock and diced leftover ham stirred through at the end is the best version of this soup. The vegetarian base recipe stands on its own, but a slice of good bread spread with butter and a bowl of this soup is a proper lunch rather than a starter.
